source.title: Selective induction Heads: How Transformers Select Causal Structures in Context
source.authors: Francesco D'Angelo; Francesco Croce; Nicolas Flammarion

page_placements.theme: Generalised and higher-order induction in toy models and theory

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study extends induction-head analysis to a new synthetic task: selecting among causal structures (Markov-chain lags) in context. It reports results on trained transformers and the resulting copying behaviour, but does not reproduce the original repeated-token induction experiment.
record.gate_note: The paper explicitly distinguishes its selective induction head from the standard induction head: the copied position is selected from evidence about the sequence’s lag, rather than by a fixed previous-token matching rule. It does not measure training-time formation, an in-context-learning loss-by-token-index effect, or a loss-curve bump. The empirical results concern next-token prediction on synthetic interleaved Markov chains, not few-shot task learning in large language models. Detailed attention-map panels for additional lag conditions and the Appendix E simulation statistics are not separately catalogued here: they either repeat the reported attention-map finding or measure a transition-probability statistic rather than transformer behaviour.
record.test_reason: The paper defines a 'selective induction head' and says it differs fundamentally from standard induction heads. It is a 3-layer circuit that picks a lag from aggregated transition-probability evidence and copies from that position. It does not use [A][B]…[A] prefix matching. All results are next-token KL and attention maps for this new circuit on synthetic interleaved Markov chains. These measure a related but different construct. No result bears on standard induction-head formation or mechanism (V1), training dynamics (V2, V7), in-context learning in large models (V3, V6), universality of induction heads (V4), or data dependence of induction-head formation (V5). The findings belong under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that 3-layer attention-only transformers solve in-context causal-structure (lag) selection with near-optimal sample complexity via selective induction heads. They describe these as a new circuit that generalizes, and differs from, standard induction heads. Trained standard and disentangled transformers align with their interpretable construction, and 2-layer models fail. The construction's estimator converges to maximum likelihood in certain cases, and Claim 1 is validated only empirically. They speculate, without testing, that the same mechanism underlies more complex reasoning in larger models.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains transformers on synthetic interleaved Markov chains with varying lags, constructs an interpretable three-layer selective-lag circuit, and evaluates next-token KL and attention maps. It does not use the original repeated-token induction-head training/loss-curve method.
record.method_sensitivity: Performance changes with depth and the number of second-layer heads: two-layer models fail; increasing second-layer heads improves performance up to the number of lags; additional heads beyond that do not improve it. Increasing depth beyond three layers does not change reported performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Trained 3-layer attention-only standard and disentangled transformers form a 'selective induction head'. Layer 3 copies the token at the in-context-selected lag. Their attention maps closely match a hand construction (layers 1 and 3 nearly identical; layer 2 similar but not identical).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Transformers trained on mixtures of causal structures learn induction-like copy heads whose copy offset is selected in context from aggregated evidence.

fits_no_version.finding: 2-layer attention-only transformers cannot solve the lag-selection task for any head configuration tested. Depth beyond 3 layers gives no further gain.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Selecting among causal structures in context requires at least three attention layers, one more than standard induction.

fits_no_version.finding: Task KL approaches maximum likelihood as second-layer heads increase up to the number of lags, with no gain beyond. The selective head still forms with fewer heads, and trained 1-head models beat the 1-head construction.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sample efficiency of selective induction scales with the number of aggregation heads.

record.problems: The evidence is limited to synthetic Markov-chain tasks and small attention-only transformers. The paper does not test standard induction heads or training-time emergence. Several empirical values are presented only in figures, without reported uncertainty. The authors leave the full proof of Claim 1 for future work and provide empirical validation for it instead.
record.rows_left_out: Figures 8–14 contain additional attention-map examples for lag conditions; omitted as repetitive figure-only instances of the selective attention pattern reported in R3–R4. Appendix E reports simulation statistics for normalized transition probabilities, not transformer behaviour, so they are not rows.

untested.parts: Standard [A][B]…[A]→[B] induction heads and composition with a previous-token head are not examined. The circuit studied is a lag-selecting copy head.
No training trajectory, abrupt formation, loss bump or concurrent in-context-learning gain is reported.
No large transformers and no loss-by-token-index in-context-learning analysis.

No survey of standard induction heads across model families, sizes, runs, architectures or modalities. Only 3-layer attention-only standard and disentangled transformers are trained, on one synthetic task.
No manipulation of training data properties measured against induction-head formation or in-context-learning persistence. Only architecture (depth, head count) versus task KL.
No few-shot task learning or comparison of head types.
Gives a static 3-layer algorithmic decomposition, not a measurement of training-time sub-steps or transitions.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests'/T3 with V4/V5 supports labels is overturned. The study's construct is explicitly a different circuit from the claim's induction head, and its V5-tagged rows measure architecture-dependent task performance, not induction-head formation. Other results not in the rows also bear on no version: Fig. 4 panels for non-contiguous lags, five lags, and two lags with one head; Fig. 7 attention maps with fewer heads; Figs. 8–14 per-lag attention maps. Could alternatively be filed as T3 if the phenomenon page counts generalized induction circuits, but under the gate rules it is a related construct. Peer-reviewed at ICLR 2025.

versions.untested_parts: The standard [A][B] … [A] → [B] mechanism and its composition with a previous-token head are not tested. The paper says its selective copying mechanism differs from the standard induction head.
No training trajectory, abrupt formation window, loss bump, or temporal coincidence with an in-context-learning gain is measured.
The study does not test whether induction heads explain most loss-by-token-index in-context learning in large transformers.

Tests trained standard and disentangled transformers only in the paper’s synthetic Markov-chain task. It does not establish universality across broad model families, training runs, modalities, or non-transformer architectures.
Tests task performance under changes to layer/head configurations and lag sets, but not when canonical induction heads form during training or whether ordinary in-context learning persists.
No few-shot task-learning mechanism or comparison with other heads for few-shot learning is tested.
The paper gives a three-layer algorithmic decomposition, but does not measure separate training transitions or test whether formation is a sequence of phases.

relation.reason: The introduction and Section 5 discuss standard induction heads and distinguish the proposed selective circuit from them; the experiments evaluate the selective circuit.

tranche.reason: The study measures selective-lag inference and copying through aggregated transition evidence, a different construct from the catalog's induction mechanism. Its results do not test a listed claim version.

source_check.notes: Exact KL values are not stated for the checked curves; figure-only entries are appropriate. The depth findings concern the tested two-, three-, four-, and five-layer configurations.
